headline: Alaska: Peltola unseats Sullivan, giving Democrats 56 Senate seats
dek: AP called Alaska's Senate race for Mary Peltola on 17 November, taking Democrats to 56 seats, the bloc that will decide cannabis banking and hemp bills in 2027.
key_points: The AP called Alaska's US Senate race for Democrat Mary Peltola on 17 November; she led Republican Sen. Dan Sullivan 50.1% to 45.8% with about 99% counted.
Because Peltola cleared 50% of first-choice votes, no ranked-choice count is needed; certification is due on 25 November.
By AP's count Democrats now hold a 56-44 Senate majority after flipping nine seats, still four short of the 60 votes that most bills need.
Peltola has backed cannabis banking reform in the past, according to The Marijuana Herald; the new Senate will inherit SAFER Banking and the hemp fight.
body: Mary Peltola, a Democrat and former congresswoman, has won Alaska's US Senate seat, defeating Republican Sen. Dan Sullivan. The Associated Press called the race on the evening of 17 November, two weeks after polling day. With 290,003 ballots counted, Peltola had 144,302 first-choice votes, or 50.1%, against 131,844, or 45.8%, for Sullivan, according to the AP's reading of the Alaska Division of Elections summary report.

The result completes the Senate picture from the 3 November midterms. Republicans went into the election with a 53-47 majority. By the AP's count Democrats now hold 56 seats to 44, after flipping nine, the most for the party since 1958. For the cannabis industry, that means the chamber that has stalled banking reform for years will be run by a different party from January, with a bigger cushion than most forecasts expected.

Alaska uses ranked-choice voting in general elections, and on election night the race looked headed for a second round. Sullivan briefly led as early returns came in. As later ballots were counted, Peltola moved ahead and then past the 50% line. Alaska Public Media reported that because she holds a majority of first-choice votes, no ranked-choice calculation is needed.

Two minor candidates split the rest: Gerald Heikes took 2.1% (6,105 votes) and a second candidate also named Dan Sullivan, listed as Dan J. Sullivan, took 1.7% (4,760). By our arithmetic, Peltola's lead over the incumbent is 12,458 votes, or 4.3 percentage points. Overseas ballots can still arrive until 18 November, and officials planned a final unofficial tabulation that evening, with certification due on 25 November. The AP estimated about 99% of votes had been counted when it made its call.

The race was not clean. Alaska Public Media and the Anchorage Daily News report that a Justice Department lawsuit to block certification was dismissed and is on appeal, and that a federal criminal investigation is looking at how the second Dan Sullivan came to be on the ballot. Peltola has denied knowing about his recruitment. Messages left with both campaigns on 17 November went unanswered, the AP said; Peltola posted a short thank-you to voters on social media.
> A 56-seat Senate does not pass cannabis bills on its own; it changes which ones get a vote.

Peltola served in the US House from 2022 until she lost her seat in 2024 to Republican Nick Begich. According to The Marijuana Herald, she was a cosponsor of the SAFE Banking Act in 2023 and told the Alaska Beacon in 2022 that she supported federal legalization. The Herald describes Sullivan as never having explicitly backed nationwide legalization. We could not independently confirm her cosponsorship record because the congressional database blocked our request, so we attribute these points to the Herald.

Alaska itself has had legal adult-use cannabis since voters approved it in 2014, and its regulators are busy this week: as we reported on 16 November, the state's Marijuana Control Board meets on 18 and 19 November to consider doubling the daily purchase limit for concentrates from 7 grams to 14 grams. A senator from a mature legal market adds another voice for operators who already pay full taxes but cannot use ordinary banks.

The arithmetic still matters more than the mood. Most bills need 60 votes to clear a filibuster, and a 56-44 chamber is four votes short of that on party lines. SAFER Banking has had Republican sponsors in past sessions, so the question for 2027 is less whether Democrats support it than whether the new majority leader puts it on the floor and finds the Republicans to pass it.

That leadership choice is still open. As we reported on 16 November, Chuck Schumer and Chris Van Hollen, the two senators competing to lead Senate Democrats, have different track records on cannabis. Peltola will be one of the incoming members who vote in that contest.

The result is also another blow for the cannabis-funded super PAC that backed House Republicans this year. As we reported on 15 November, 13 of the 14 incumbents it supported lost their seats and the 14th race, in Alaska, was still uncalled. That race is Begich's House seat, and the AP had not yet called it on 17 November.

Peltola does not take her seat until January, so the decisions due this year fall to the current Senate. The biggest is the federal hemp restriction due on 11 December, when the current stopgap funding law expires. Lawmakers in both parties want to attach hemp language to the next funding bill; whether they do so before the deadline will shape the hemp market long before the new majority sits.

Watch the final unofficial tabulation on 18 November and certification on 25 November, plus the appeal of the Justice Department's certification lawsuit. Watch the AP call in Alaska's House race between Begich and independent Bill Hill. In the Senate, watch the Democratic leadership vote and whether SAFER Banking is named as an early priority, and in Anchorage, the Marijuana Control Board's decision on concentrate limits this week.
